parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin -iscus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad poenam, with an additional adverbial /-s/ (compare doncs < Latin tunc).
From a- + baixar. Cognate with Galician and Portuguese abaixar.
Inherited from Old Catalan abants, from Vulgar Latin *abantius, from Late Latin ab ante (with /-(i)us/ added perhaps by analogy with prius), from ab (“from”) + ante (“before”). Compare Occitan abans.
From Vulgar Latin *abbellīre.

parole.significato: to give water (chiefly to an animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abbiberāre, ultimately derived from Latin bibere (“drink”). Could be analyzed as a- + beure + -ar, but cf. the numerous Romance cognates.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abȳssimus, superlative of abyssus.
From a- + braç (“arm”) + -ar, from Old Catalan, from Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. Compare Occitan acabar.
From a- + *canís + -ar, from Vulgar Latin *canicius, from canis (“dog”).
From Vulgar Latin *accapitare.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *clūdĭcāre (“to close”). Compare with Aragonese clucar and Occitan clucar~cluchar with the same meaning
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, from Latin ad- + colligere.
Inherited from Old Catalan acomparar, from Vulgar Latin *accomparāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(ac)complīre, from Latin complēre.

parole.significato: to arrive (at a place), to get (to a place)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōnsequīre, or *cōnsequere, from Latin cōnsequor.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accordāre.

parole.significato: to arrange artfully; to dress, trim
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *comptiare. Compare Italian acconciare and Aragonese acunzar.
Inherited from Old Catalan aco, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hoc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adderēctus, from ad- + derēctus.
Inherited from Old Catalan, from Vulgar Latin *drēctiāre (compare Occitan adreçar, French adresser, syncopated form of *dīrēctiāre, from Latin dīrēctus. First attested in the 14th century.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addessum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affactare, from Latin affectāre. Doublet of afectar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adferrāre, from ferrum (“iron, sword”). By surface analysis, a- + ferro + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affōcāre, alteration of Latin offōcāre. Doublet of ofegar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, from Latin ad frontem.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aggreviāre, *aggraviāre, variant form(s) of Latin aggravō. Equivalent to a- + greu + -jar.
Old Catalan aguar, from Vulgar Latin *acūtiāre, derived from Latin acūtus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *asciāta, from ascia (“axe”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *axella, from Late Latin ascella, from Latin axilla. Compare Occitan aissèla, French aisselle, Italian ascella. Doublet of axil·la, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc, from Latin eccum + sīc. Cognate with Sicilian accussì and Italian così. Compare also Portuguese assim, Romanian așa, Spanish así, French ainsi.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin albicina, from Latin albicō (“to make white”).
From Vulgar Latin *apiliāgō, from apis (“bee”) and the suffix -āgō, common in plant names.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *albuciōnem, from Latin albūcus.

parole.significato: then, back then, in those times
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin ad illās hōrās (“at those hours”). Compare Occitan alara, French alors, Italian allora, Spanish alora.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alicūnus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *altīvus.
From Vulgar Latin ilicīna. Compare Spanish encina (“evergreen oak”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).

Uncertain, there are several proposals made for its origin: * From Vulgar Latin *admānsiōnāre, a Compound of ad + mānsiō, cognate with Occitan amainà and Old French amaisnier; * Less likely, from Gothic *𐌰𐍆𐌼𐌰𐌲𐌹𐌽𐍉𐌽 (*afmaginōn, “to lose strength”), a Compound of 𐌰𐍆 (af) + 𐌼𐌰𐌲𐌰𐌽 (magan, “to be able”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ēmerāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *admināciāre < *mināciāre, a verb based on Latin minācia (“threat”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amindla, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Doublet of amígdala and màndorla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”).
Vulgar Latin *admortīre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”). By surface analysis, amor + -ós.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hanca, from Proto-Germanic *hankō (related to *ankijǭ (“joint, limb”)). Cognate with English haunch.
Probably from Vulgar Latin ambĭtātŏrium, *ambĭtātŏrius, from *ambitāre (“to go around”).
From Vulgar Latin agōnia with influence from angoixa.
Deverbal from *antostar, from Vulgar Latin *antobstare (“to put up”), from ante- and obstō.

parole.significato: to apperceive, to be aware of, to understand the significance of
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appercipere, from Latin ad- + percipiō. Equivalent to a- + percebre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum ipse, from Latin eccum + ipse.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from a compound of Latin eccum and ille.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum + iste. Compare Occitan aquest and Spanish aqueste.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc, from Latin eccum + hīc ("this here"), the latter from hīc, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi-ḱe (“this, here”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aes.

parole.significato: to mast (fit with masts and rigging)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *arborare, from Latin arbor (“tree”). Compare Italian alberare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arbuciu, from Latin arbuteus (“of the strawberry tree”), from arbutus (“strawberry tree”). Compare French arbousier, Occitan arboça.

parole.significato: a sandy place, such as a sandbank, a sand dune, a sandy beach, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin arēnĕum, from arēna (“sand”).
From Vulgar Latin *arganellum, diminutive of *arganum (“capstan”), variation of organum (“instrument, tool”). Cognate with Spanish arganeo (“anchor ring”) and French arganeau (“anchor ring”).
From Vulgar Latin *oiācem, from Ancient Greek οἴᾱκος (oíākos). The initial ar- may be due to influence from words of Arabic origin with an initial article.
From arc + -er or Vulgar Latin *arcārius, from Latin arcuārius, from arcus (“bow”) + -arius (relational suffix). Compare Occitan arquièr and Spanish arquero.
From dissimilation of earlier *arreorir, from Vulgar Latin *adrigōrīre or *inrigōrīre, from Latin rigor.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“stand”). Compare Occitan arrestar and French arrêter.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrare, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”).
Variant form of sossegar, from earlier *sessegar, from Vulgar Latin *sessicāre, from sessus, perfect passive participle of sedeō. Cognate with Portuguese sossegar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin acceptōrem, modification of Latin accipiter (“hawk”).
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *attinctiāre, from attinctus, innovative past particle of attingō (“to touch, I arrive at”).

parole.significato: to stoke (to feed, stir up, especially, a fire or furnace)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *attītiāre, derived from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin ossifrangēns, from Latin ossifragus (“osprey”), literally "bone-breaking".

parole.significato: a tree of the genus Acer, a maple tree
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *acerone, from Latin acer.
Inherited from Old Catalan auantatge, from Vulgar Latin *abantāticum. By surface analysis, avant (“forward, ahead”) + -atge.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre (“move forward”), from Late Latin ab ante, from ab + ante.
From Vulgar Latin *adventūra, from Late Latin adventurus, from Latin adventus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *advitiāre, from *vitiāre (“accustom, habituate”), from Latin vitium. Compare Spanish avezar and vezar, Portuguese vezar and avezar, Occitan avezar and envezar, Italian avvezzare, and Romanian învăța.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abētem, from Classical Latin abietem.

parole.significato: a basin, particularly a barber's bowl (a type of wide basin with a notch in it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“wide bowl”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre, from Late Latin bassus (“low; short”).
From Old Catalan baladrar + -ejar, from Vulgar Latin *balatrare. Compare Spanish baladrar, Portuguese bradar.
Alteration of earlier balbuçar, from Vulgar Latin *balbūtiāre, a variant of Latin balbūtiō (“to stutter, stammer”).
Alteration of earlier baldritxa, from Vulgar Latin *pardice, from Latin perdix (“partridge”).
From Vulgar Latin *pardice, from Latin perdix (“partridge”).
From Vulgar Latin *barbalionis, modification of barba (“beard”) Iovis (“of Jupiter”), a name anciently applied to butcher's broom.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *barbūtus. By surface analysis, barba + -ut.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *barra, possibly from Gaulish *barros (“the bushy end”), cognate with French barre and English bar. Doublet of bar.
From Vulgar Latin *persidia, from Ancient Greek (σφενδόνη) περσῐ́ς ((sphendónē) persĭ́s, “Persian (sling)”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastaxus, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to bear, carry”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastāre (“to suffice”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastōnem, variant of Latin bastum.

parole.significato: clapper (an object suspended inside a bell)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bat(t)uāculum, from Latin bat(t)uere (“beat”). Compare Occitan batalh.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *battucula, plural of *battuculum, variant form of *battuāculum, from battuō (“to beat”). Doublet of batall.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *baba, of infantile/nursery origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *betullus, from Latin betulla, from Gaulish *betua, from Proto-Celtic *betwiyos, *betuyā (“birch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-.
Equivalent to bell + -esa, possibly from Vulgar Latin *bellitia, from Latin bellus. Compare Italian bellezza, Portuguese beleza, Occitan belesa, and Spanish belleza.

parole.significato: to move, to shift, to fidget
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bullicāre (with vowel metathesis), a frequentative based on bullīre.

parole.significato: welcome (to a male or person of unknown gender)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, ben (“well”) + vingut (“come”).
From earlier bertol, contraction of *vertó(v)ol, from Vulgar Latin vertibulum, diminutive of Latin vertebra.

Uncertain. Compare Occitan besugue (“crosseyed”), Portuguese besugo (“seabream”), Spanish besugo (“blackspot seabream”). Perhaps, like Spanish bisojo (“crosseyed”), derived from a Vulgar Latin *bisoculus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bisonium. Compare Occitan besonh, French besoin and Italian bisogno.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bittūmen, from Latin bitūmen.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bettius, from Proto-Celtic *betwiyos. Compare also Occitan beç and Middle Welsh bedw.

parole.significato: a type of small double-horned anvil used mainly by blacksmiths and tinsmiths
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan bigòrnia, bicòrnia, from a Vulgar Latin *bicŏrnĭa (“anvil”), from Latin bicornis (“two-horned”) nominalized in the feminine with -a.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *buccīnum, from bucca (“cheek, mouth”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volvicāre, from Latin volvere.
From Vulgar Latin *bulbulla, from Latin bulliō (“to bubble, to boil”) (from which bullir).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bonacia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bulbulliāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burrula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bornium.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *borrasicare, from Late Latin borrās (“north wind”), from Ancient Greek Βορρᾶς (Borrhâs).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *boscāticum. Equivalent to bosc + -atge.
Perhaps ultimately from Vulgar Latin *butticellus, diminutive of buttis (“barrel”).
From Vulgar Latin *brandus, from Frankish *brand.

parole.significato: to brandish (to move a weapon back and forth)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *brandus, from Frankish *brand.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brandīre, from *brandus, from Frankish *brand.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus. Compare Italian bravo.
From Vulgar Latin berciolum, diminutive of *bertium, from Gaulish *berta (compare Old Irish bert (“bundle”)). Cognate with French berceau.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bertiāre, from Gaulish *berta (compare Old Irish bert (“bundle”)). Cognate with French bercer, Occitan breçar and Spanish brezar and brizar.
From Vulgar Latin berciolum diminutive of *bertium, from Gaulish *berta, from Proto-Celtic *bertā, variant of *bereti (“to carry”). Compare Old Irish bert (“bundle”). Cognate with French berceau.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin brocca, from broccus (“having projecting teeth”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brustāre, from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌶𐌳𐍉𐌽 (*bruzdōn), from Proto-Germanic *bruzdōną. Compare Spanish bordar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *broglāre, from Proto-Germanic *brogilos.
Variation of brollar, from Inherited from Vulgar Latin *broglāre.
Alteration of Vulgar Latin buxida (“box”) with influence from Latin capsula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *būcāta, from Frankish *būkō (“to submerge; to wash”). Cognate with French buée and Italian bucato.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vocitum.
From Vulgar Latin *bustiola, *buxiola, diminutive of Latin buxis (“box”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burdicāre, influenced by punxar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capittia, variant of capitia, plural of Latin capitium.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin caprītus (attested in Salic Law), from *caprīre, from Latin caper. Compare Occitan cabrit and cabrida, Spanish cabrito, Portuguese cabrito, dialectal French chevri.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum. Compare Italian catafalco.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin cathégra (compare Occitan cadièra, Portuguese cadeira, Lombard cadrega), from Latin cathedra (compare French chaire, whence also English chair), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “above”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “chair”). Doublet of the borrowing càtedra.

parole.significato: A natural hollow or depression in a rocky surface where water collects.
parole.testo: Uncertain; perhaps from Vulgar Latin *catulla, probably influenced by Proto-Celtic *tullos (“hollow”).

parole.significato: quarrel (bolt for an arbalest or crossbow)
parole.testo: Either directly from Vulgar Latin *quadrellus, a diminutive of quadrus, or from caire + -ell.

parole.significato: to tread on, to step on
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calcīcāre, from calx (“heel”).

parole.significato: to heat up, to warm up (to cause to become hotter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calidizāre. Derivable from cald + -ejar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calfāre, from Latin cal(e)facere. Compare French chauffer.
From Vulgar Latin *calivum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calandria, from Ancient Greek χαραδριός (kharadriós, “stone-curlew”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, camí + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin cammīnus (“way”) (compare Occitan camin, French chemin, Spanish camino), from Gaulish.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cannabācea, feminine of *cannabāceus (“hempen”), from cannabis.
From Vulgar Latin *canālia, possibly via Italian canaglia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *candelubrum, from Latin candēlābrum. First attested in the 13th century.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *canīlia, collective based on Latin canis (“a dog”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre, of Gaulish origin. Compare Occitan cambiar, French changer, Spanish cambiar.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus (“head, chief”), from Latin caput (“head, etc.”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *káput. Compare Occitan cap. Compare also French personne (which can mean either "person" or "nobody").
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cappulare.
From Vulgar Latin *capitiare, from Latin capitium (“head covering”).
From Vulgar Latin *capĭtiōne, from Latin capitium (“head covering”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō.
Alteration of cardina, from Vulgar Latin *carduīna, from carduus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carnūtus, derived from Latin carnem (“meat”). By surface analysis, carn + -ut.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *carrīlis, as an alteration of Late Latin currīlis, from Latin currus (“chariot”), with influence from carrus.
Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *carōnia. First attested in the 19th century, and on that basis, probably borrowed from Italian carogna. Compare English carrion.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quassicāre, frequentative from Latin quassāre (“strike”).
From Vulgar Latin cascābellus (“small bell”), diminutive of cascābus, from Latin cāccabus. Compare Occitan cascavèl.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cassanilla, from Gaulish kassanos (“oak”). Related to French chêne.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus.

parole.significato: a cold north or northwest wind
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cercius, variation of Latin circius (“west-northwest wind”), from Ancient Greek κίρκιος (kírkios).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cicerōnem, derived from Latin cicer.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cymbellum, diminutive of Latin cymbalum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cingellum, from Latin cingulum (“girdle”). Doublet of cingle.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin ceresia (compare Occitan cerièra), from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clavācāria, derived from Late Latin clavāca, variant of Latin cloāca.

parole.significato: peg (cylindrical wooden or metal object used as a bearing between two objects)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clāvicla, from Latin clāvicula (“bolt”). Doublet of clavícula, a borrowing from Latin.

parole.significato: trammel (set of rings or other hanging devices, used to hang cooking pots etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan cremascles, Vulgar Latin *cremastulum, from Ancient Greek κρεμαστήρ (kremastḗr, “suspender”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cuperāre (“take, seize”), a back-formation from Latin recuperāre (“recover, regain”), whence Catalan recobrar. Doublet of recuperar, a borrowing from Latin.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coopercellum, diminutive of Latin cooperculum (“a covering”), influenced by cel (the expected result would have been *cobercell). Compare Occitan cobercel and cobrecel or French couverceau.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coxīnum from coxa (“thigh”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare French colle, Portuguese and Spanish cola, Italian colla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *colātīcius, from Latin colāre. By surface analysis, colat + -ís.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coleūtus (“betesticled”), derived from Latin cōleus (“testicle”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *colŏbra, altered from Classical Latin colubra, feminine counterpart to coluber (“snake”), of uncertain origin. Compare Occitan colòbra, French couleuvre, and Spanish culebra. Doublet of cobra, which was borrowed from Portuguese.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quomō, from classical Latin quōmodō. Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese como. See also French comme and Italian come.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō. First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: to communicate (to give or receive Holy Communion)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *comminicāre, from Latin commūnicāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre.

parole.significato: to pity, to feel sorry for
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *compatīre, an active counterpart to Latin compatior. Cognate with Italian compatire.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *compānia, a collective noun based on Late Latin compāniō (“comrade”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *complīre, from Latin complēre. The past participle complert is analogous.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”). Compare Occitan crompar, Spanish comprar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *condīrēctus, from con- + dīrēctus.
From a Vulgar Latin root *conquerīre, from Latin conquīrere (compare Occitan conquerir, French conquérir, Romanian cuceri).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *conredāre, from Latin con- (“with; together”) + a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *raidaz (“ready, prepared”). Cognate with Old French correer, source of English curry (“to groom, to dress”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contrāta. Compare Italian contrada, French contrée.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *convītāre, from Latin invītāre (“to invite”). Compare Occitan and Portuguese convidar and French convier.
Inherited from Old Catalan cor, from Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corāticum. Attested in the Homilies d'Organyà.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cordellus, diminutive of Latin chorda (“rope, cord”). Equivalent to corda + -ell.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *cordārium. The DCVB argue that it is borrowed from Spanish cordero on the following grounds: it is not attested in Catalan until the fifteenth century, it has existed from the beginning alongside a Castilian-like variant cordero, and its distribution is limited to weste
Variant form of cordell, from Vulgar Latin *cordellus.
Substantivization of Vulgar Latin *curritīcia (“prone to running”), from Latin currere.

parole.significato: sliding, able to made to glide
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *curriticium, from Latin currere.
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *currōnem, derived from Latin currus (“chariot”).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *cusculicula, diminutive of Latin cusculium (“berry of the holm oak”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cosīre, from Latin cōnsuere, with normal change of conjugation to -ir.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *cauceus, from Late Latin caucus (“goblet”).
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *cauciolus, from *caucellus, diminutive of caucus, with a change of suffix.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōnsūtūra, from Latin cōnsūtus, from consuō.

Uncertain. Suggestions include: # From cosa (“thing”) + -ó (“augmentative ending”). # From Balearic cus (“small dog”) + -ó (“diminutive ending”), possibly related to gos (“dog”). # From Vulgar Latin *cociō, diminutive of cocus (“cook”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cutina, from Latin cutis (“skin, rind”).
From Vulgar Latin *cova, itself an alteration of Late Latin cava (or of a Vulgar Latin *covum, *covus), from Latin cavus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crepantare, derived from Latin crepāre (“rattle”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.
Vulgar Latin *cruscīre, from Frankish *krustijan. Compare Spanish crujir, Old French croissir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crucīcula, from crux.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coquīnārium, or a later formation corresponding to cuina + -er.
From Vulgar Latin *coctāre, from Latin *cōctus, from coactus, past participle of cōgō. Cognate with Portuguese coitar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cultīvus, from Latin cultus.
Uncertain. Perhaps related to daga (“dagger”) via a proposed Vulgar Latin *dacula.
From Vulgar Latin *dantiāre.
Probably from an original *darrerer, from Vulgar Latin *deretrārius. By surface analysis, darrere + -er.

parole.significato: to reel (wind on a reel), to wind
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *depānāre, from pānus (“thread wound upon the bobbin”).

parole.significato: to decline, to deteriorate (to become weaker or worse)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, from Latin dēcidere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēexaptāre (“undo, untie”), from dē- + *exaptāre from ex- + aptō (“to fasten, to fit”). Cognate with Spanish desatar.
Variant of deixondar, from Vulgar Latin *dēexsomnitāre, from somnus (“sleep”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēlērium, alteration of Latin dēlīrium (“madness”). Doublet of deliri, a learned borrowing.
Inherited from Old Catalan deena, from Vulgar Latin decena, from Latin decēnus (“tenth”). More at desè.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpendĕre, from Classical Latin dēpendēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *discaballicāre. By surface analysis, des- + cavalcar.

parole.significato: to get rid of, to shake off
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan *desempeegar, Vulgar Latin *disimpedicāre, from impedicāre.

From the noun desig; cf. Latin dēsīderō, dēsīderāre (“long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin verb *dēsidiāre, itself perhaps a crossing between Latin dēsīderāre and invidiāre, from invidia. Compare Occitan desirar and Portuguese desejar, Spanish de

Probably from Vulgar Latin *exmagāre (“deprive of power or strength”), from ex- + *magare (“to enable; empower”), from Frankish *magan, *mugan (“to be able”), from Proto-Germanic *maganą. Compare Old French esmaier, Old Occitan esmaiar, Portuguese esmagar, Spanish amagar, Spanish esmayar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin de + *expertus for Latin experrectus. Compare Spanish despierto.
From Vulgar Latin *expertāre, from *expertus, from Latin experrēctus (“awoken”), perfect passive participle of expergīscor (“to awake, to wake up”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dia, from Latin diēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Compare Gascon dia and Spanish día.
From Old Catalan dinar, from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre, from Late Latin disieiūnō (“to break the fast”), from dis- + ieiūnō (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus. Compare Occitan disnar, French dîner.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dīnārius, an alteration of Latin dēnārius. Doublet of dinar and denari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin decem novem, from Latin decem (“ten”) et (“and”) novem (“nine”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin dē intus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin decem septem, from Latin decem (“ten”) et (“and”) septem (“seven”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin decem octō, from Latin decem (“ten”) et (“and”) octō (“eight”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dullia, a borrowing of Frankish *dullī (“pipe, tube, conduit”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin dunc (with adverbial /-s/), probably from a crossing of Latin tunc with dum. Compare Occitan dunc, French donc, Italian dunque, and also Spanish entonces, Portuguese então, Romanian atunci.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *domnicellus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, diminutive of *domna, from Latin domina.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exhancāre, from *hanca (“haunch”).
From Vulgar Latin *exsarculare, from Late Latin sarculō (“I hoe”).
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *exēreptus, from ēripiō (“to snatch”).

parole.significato: to clear for planting, to bring into cultivation
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exeremāre, from Latin erē̆mus.

parole.significato: to pluck the eyes out of; to blind
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exorbāre, from orbus.
From Vulgar Latin *imbŭcciare. By surface analysis, em- + boç + -ar.
Inherited from Old Catalan amparar, from Vulgar Latin *anteparāre (“to prevent”), from Latin ante- + parō, parāre.

parole.significato: to graft (to insert in a branch or stem of another tree)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *empeltāre, from *emputāre, from Latin imputāre.

From a substantivation of the feminine of Old Catalan empent (the original past participle of empènyer), from Vulgar Latin *impinctus, as an alternative past participle of Latin impingō (instead of the Classical participle impāctus). The Vulgar Latin form would have ordinarily yielded a Catalan *emp
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, from Latin prehendere.
By surface analysis, en- + cabestre (“halter”) + -ar, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *incapistrāre.
From Vulgar Latin *incalciāre, derived from Latin calx (“heel”).
From Vulgar Latin hanc hōram (“at this hour”). Compare French encore, Italian ancora.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre. By surface analysis, en- + carregar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incīsāmen, collective of incīsum, from incīdō (“to cut into”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inclaudere, remodelled from Latin inclūdere. Doublet of incloure, which was borrowed. By surface analysis, en- + cloure.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indulcīre, derived from Latin dulcis (“sweet”, adjective). By surface analysis, en- + dolç + -ir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indīrēctiāre, from *dīrēctiāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inimicitātem.

parole.significato: to deceive, to fool, to mislead
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō. First attested in the 12th century. Compare Occitan enganar, Spanish engañar, Old French engignier.
From en- + *gargús + -ar, from a presumed Vulgar Latin *gurgutia related to gurguliō (“gullet”). Influenced in form by gargall (“phlegm”).

Numerous derivations have been proposed, including: # from a Vulgar Latin *exiacicāre, from *iacium (“bed, bedding”) (source of jaç), from Latin iaceō (“to lie”); # from an Andalusi Arabic form of Arabic تَشَكَّى (tašakkā), frequentive/intensive of شَكَا (šakā, “to complain”) (source of xacra); # fr
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hōque annō, from Latin hōc annō. Probably influenced by the prefix en-. Cognate to Occitan ongan.
From Vulgar Latin *innōdicāre, from Latin innōdō (“to tie in a knot”), from nōdus (“knot”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also found in Medieval Latin) (compare Occitan ensenhar, French enseigner, Spanish enseñar), from Latin signāre.
Derived from Vulgar Latin *assōpīre with a change of suffix; ultimately from Latin sōpīre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īnsurctus, innovative past participle of Latin īnsurgō.
From en- + terra + -ar or Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin terra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *anteoculāre, from oculus (“eye”).
From Vulgar Latin in tōrnō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *intortiliāre, from Latin tortilis (“twisted, coiled”). Compare Spanish entortijar, French entortiller.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intercoxium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *invādīre, from Latin invādere.
From earlier envolopar, from a reconstructed Vulgar Latin *involuppare. Compare French envelopper.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aequilībrāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ērīciōnem, from Latin ēricius, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“to bristle”). Compare Occitan eriçon.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *erctus, equivalent of Latin ērectus. Doublet of erecte, a learned borrowing.

Inherited from Old Catalan esbalausir, from Vulgar Latin *exblaudīre, ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *blauþijaną (“to make weak, make void, soften”). Cognate with French éblouir (“to dazzle”).

parole.significato: to cleave, to split, to splinter
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from an unattested Vulgar Latin *exvirgulāre from virgula (“small rod or twig”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excalfare, from Classical Latin excalfacere. Equivalent to es- + calfar. Cognate with English chafe.
From Vulgar Latin *scandāculum, probably via Old Occitan escandalh or Ligurian scandaglio. Cognate to Spanish escandallo.
From Vulgar Latin *excambiāre. By surface analysis, es- + canviar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).
From Vulgar Latin *cappulare, from Latin capulō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excapitiāre, from caput; influenced in form by capitium (source of cabeç).
Deverbal from escarnir, from Vulgar Latin *escarnire representing Proto-Germanic *skarnjan. Cognate with Portuguese escárnio, Spanish escarnio and Italian scherno.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *scatta, attested as scatus, squato and squatam, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: to suit (to be suitable or apt)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excadĕre. By surface analysis, es- + caure.

parole.significato: tree pit (excavated area around an urban tree)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caucellus, diminutive of caucus (“goblet”).

parole.significato: to sweep, sweep away, sweep out
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *excomborāre, from a proposed Proto-Celtic *comboros. This could be from the same root underlying Medieval Latin combrus (“barricade of felled trees”), reconstructed as Gaulish *komberū, from Proto-Celtic *kombereti (“to bring together”) (from *kom- + *bereti (“to bear”))
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scoculum, from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excūrāre (“to clean”), from cūrāre (“to look after”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excurtiare, from curtus (“short”).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *excurtiōnem, from Late Latin curtiō, from Latin curtus (“short”). Compare Spanish escuerzo, dialectal Italian scorzone, Sicilian scursuni, Mozarabic uxcurchón.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scalamus, from scalmus, from Ancient Greek σκαλμός (skalmós, “pin, thole”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excarsus, from Late Latin excarpsus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfunderāre. Compare French effondrer.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, ultimately from Latin fortis (“strong”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exgladiāre, from Latin gladius.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *admorticīre (with the prefix replaced by es-), variant form of *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”).

parole.significato: to breakfast (first meal of the day)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *admordium (“breakfast”), from Latin admordēre (“snack”), but taking a verbal form to complete the series esmorzar, dinar (“to lunch”), berenar (“to have an afternoon snack”), sopar (“to have supper”).

From older espaventar, from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present active participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Occitan, Spanish, and Portuguese espantar, Italian spaventare, French épouvanter.

parole.significato: Spanish (pertaining to Spain or the Spanish language)
parole.testo: Derived from Vulgar Latin *Hispāniolus, from Latin Hispānus, from Hispānia. Compare Spanish español.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *spariliō, from Latin sparus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spatula (“flat piece”), diminutive of Latin spatha (“straight sword”). Compare Occitan espatla, French épaule, Spanish espalda (“back”). Doublet of espàtula, a borrowing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present active participle of Classical Latin expaveō, from pavor (“fear”). Compare French épouvanter, Italian spaventare.

parole.significato: to pluck fruit (from a tree, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expiluc(i)cāre, ultimately from Latin pilāre (“remove hair”). By surface analysis, es- + pellucar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Corresponds to esperar + -ança. Compare Old Occitan esperanssa.
Perhaps from earlier *esprenalla, dissimilated form of Vulgar Latin *splenalia, from Ancient Greek σπλήν (splḗn, “spleen”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *speclum (compare Occitan espelh, Spanish espejo), from syncopation of Latin speculum. Compare the borrowed doublet espècul.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin spelūca, variant form of spelunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx, “cave”).
Metathesis of obsolete espulgar, from Vulgar Latin *expūlicare, from pūlex (“flea”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excapsiāre, literally "to break a box", from capsa (“box, case”). Compare Sicilian scasciari (“split apart”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exquīntiāre (“break into five pieces”), from quīntus (“fifth”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin scūriolus, a diminutive of scūrius, metathesized variant of Latin sciūrus, ultimately from Ancient Greek σκίουρος (skíouros). Compare Occitan esquirou, Aragonese esquirol and esquiruelo, and Italian scoiattolo.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin *stēlum, from an interpretation of stēla (from Classical Latin stēlla) as a neuter plural, through analogy with other words such as Latin signa, sidera, and astra, respective neuter plurals of signum, sidus, and astrum. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. See al

parole.significato: rockrose (any of various flowering plants in the genus Cistus)
parole.testo: From a Hispanic Vulgar Latin *stippa of uncertain, probably pre-Roman origin.
Inherited from Old Catalan estubar (“to steam”), from Vulgar Latin *extūpare. Perhaps influenced in form by Italian stufare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sturnellus, from Latin sturnus.

parole.significato: to keep (in a case, box); to box up, to put away
parole.testo: Earlier estojar; from Vulgar Latin *studiare, from Latin studium. Doublet of estudiar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvadĕre, from Latin ēvādō. Doublet of evadir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvānīre, from Latin ēvānēscō with a change of prefix. Cognate with French évanouir.
From Vulgar Latin excentricus.
From Vulgar Latin *Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate, destiny told by the gods”). Compare French fée, Italian fata, Occitan and Portuguese fada, Spanish hada.
Probably Vulgar Latin *fratrīnus, diminutive of frater (“brother”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fāgīna (“beech marten”).
Apparently from a Vulgar Latin *fabeolum, masculinized diminutive of Latin faba (“bean”); probably formed by analogy with phaseolus (whence Catalan fesol).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *filicāria (“thicket of ferns”), from Latin filix (“fern”). Compare Aragonese falaguera, feleguera, Occitan falguièra, French fougère, Galician folgueira.

parole.significato: constructions of inflammable materials, based in figures that are caricatures (the ninots) that are installed in certai…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *facla, contracted form of Latin facula, diminutive of fax (“torch”). Compare the borrowed doublet fàcula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *falliāre, from Latin fallere (and so related to Catalan fallir). Compare Occitan falhar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fallita, feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō. Compare Occitan fauta, Portuguese and Spanish falta, French faute.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *fellaria, the name of a disease, from Latin fel (“gall, gallbladder”). First attested in 1803.
From Vulgar Latin *fangus ~ *fanga (“mud”) of Germanic origin, see there for more.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *faraliōne, via metathesis from Ancient Greek φαλαριῶν (phalariôn), from φάλαρος (phálaros, “having a white spot”).
Uncertain, perhaps from Vulgar Latin *flagrorare, from frāgrō (“to smell of”). Compare Occitan farigola.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fēbelis, from Latin flēbilis (“tearful, mournful, lamentable”) by dissimilation, from fleō (“to weep”) (akin to fluō (“to flow”)).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.
From Vulgar Latin *femita, from Latin fimus.
From Vulgar Latin *findicŭla, deverbal of *findiculare (etymon of French fendiller), a derivative of Latin findō , findere (“I cleave”).

parole.significato: any of various grasses in the genus Brachypodium, particularly Brachypodium distachyon or Brachypodium pinnatum
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fēnāceum, from faenum (“hay”). Compare French fenasse, Romanian fânaț.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *feroticus, from Latin ferus (“wild, savage”).

parole.significato: bolt (metal bar used to hold a door shut)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, variant form of Latin vericulum, diminutive of veru (“spit, javelin”). Influenced in form by ferro (“iron”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre. Derivable from festa + -ejar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *facticula, a derivative of factus parallel to facticius, which is the source of Spanish hechizo, Portuguese feitiço, etc.
Inherited from Old Catalan feu, from Vulgar Latin *feus, from Frankish *fehu, from Proto-Germanic *fehu.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere (“to trust”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīca, from Latin fīcus. Compare Occitan figa or higa.
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *vīmināre, from vīmen (“twig”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *[petra] fīcta, from Latin petra (“stone”) and figere (“to fix in place”).
From Vulgar Latin fīctōria, from fīctus, alternative forms of fīxus.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *fīctōne, from *fīctus (“fixed”), archaic past participle of fīgō (“to fasten, to fix”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *flabeolum, diminutive of Latin flabrum (“gust”) from flare (“to blow”). Cognate with French flageolet.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin flāgrāre, by dissimilation from Latin frāgrāre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₂gro-, from *bʰreh₂g- (“to smell”) + *-ro-. Compare Occitan flairar, French flairer, Portuguese cheirar, Sicilian ciagurari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *flammizāre, from Latin flamma. Derivable from flama (“flame”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fluruncus, metathesized form of Latin furunculus.

parole.significato: a depression or hollow in the sea floor
parole.testo: From fons + -era, or directly from Vulgar Latin *fundāria.
From formiga + -er, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Portuguese formigueiro, Spanish hormiguero, Italian formicaio, Romanian furnicar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, diminutive of furnus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, from Late Latin fortia, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, força + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frāgula, diminutive of Latin frāga, plural of frāgum.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frictiare, from Latin fricāre (“to rub”). Originally this described the action of some animals who rub their bellies on the ground while laying eggs and from there was extended to "lay eggs, spawn" in general. Doublet of fressar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *friscum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frictiāre, from Latin fricāre (“to rub”). Cognate with Spanish frisar.
Alteration of frissar, from Vulgar Latin *frictiāre, from Latin fricō (“to rub”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to flee”). Cognates include Occitan fugir, French fuir, Italian fuggire, Sicilian fùjiri, Spanish huir, Portuguese fugir, Romanian fugi.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūmizāre. Derivable from fum + -ejar. Doublet of fumigar, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūra, fūrō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūricāre, from Latin fūr (“thief”).

From Vulgar Latin (baculus) *caiatus (“cudgel-like (stick)”), from Latin caia (“cudgel”). The form (with medial i instead of expected j) may be due to influence from Mozarabic or Aragonese. Compare Spanish cayado.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin galleta, diminutive of *galla (“vessel”), possibly from Gaulish galla (“vessel”), source of English gallon. Compare Romanian găleată.
From Old Catalan galta~gauta, from Vulgar Latin *ga(v)ota.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gargantiōnem, from garganta.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin gargarismus, from Latin gargarisma.
From earlier *garolla, from Vulgar Latin *carulia, diminutive of Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon, “kernel”).

parole.significato: shank (the part of the leg between the knee and the ankle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *garra (compare Occitan garra, Spanish garra), borrowed from Gaulish *garrā (“leg”). Compare Breton gar, Old Irish gairri (“calves”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gemicāre, from Latin gemere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin ienuārius, from Latin Iānuārius. Compare Occitan genièr, French janvier, Spanish enero.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin germānus (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“of siblings”). Compare Spanish hermano.
From earlier llibrell by dissimilation, from Vulgar Latin *labrellum, diminutive of lābrum (“bathtub, basin”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of glaça.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of glaç.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *guleus, from gula (“throat”), or a blend of coll (“testicle”) + gola (“throat”).

parole.significato: only used in de gom a gom
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *culumus, metathesised form of Classical Latin cumulus. Compare Spanish colmo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gurgus, from Latin gurges (“whirlpool, eddy”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gurga, from Latin gurges (“whirlpool, eddy”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gottus, from Latin guttus. Cognate with Italian gotto, Ladin got, Occitan gòt, Venetan goto.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *gutturiō, in which case cognate with French goitron.

parole.significato: a wide step, especially one large enough to sit on; bleacher
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grada, collective of gradus (“step”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gracla (compare Occitan gralha, Italian gracchia), syncopated form of Late Latin grācula (“female jackdaw”) (compare French grolle), feminine form of Latin grāculus (compare Spanish grajo), from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Doublet of graula.

parole.significato: broom (North-Western Catalan and all Valencian dialects)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin granarĭa, with the same meaning, derived from Latin grānum ‘grain’, due to the function of gathering and removing grains from the threshing floor. Compare with Occitan engranièra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rānucula, diminutive of Latin rāna.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin grāgula, variant form of Late Latin grācula. Doublet of gralla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crassia, from Latin crassus (“thick”). Compare French graisse.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cronticāre, northern variation of Vulgar Latin *crontiare, from a Proto-Celtic or Pre-Indo-European root.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grossiēs, from Latin grossus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grumuculus, variant of Latin grumulus, diminutive of grūmus (“small heap”). Equivalent to grum + -oll. Doublet of grúmol.
Borrowed from Sicilian and Old Neapolitan grutta, from Vulgar Latin *grupta or *crupta, from Latin crypta. Doublet of cripta.

parole.significato: a holly, particularly the common European holly (Ilex aquifolium)
parole.testo: From earlier agrèvol, from Vulgar Latin *acrifolum, from Latin acrifolium, a variant of aquifolium (“pointy-leafed [plant], holly”).

parole.significato: to win (gain a prize by succeeding)
parole.testo: From earlier Old Catalan guadanyar /guasanyar /guaanyar, from Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre a borrowing from Germanic. Cognate with Occitan ganhar (medieval gazanhar, gaaigniar), French gagner, Italian guadagnare; cf. also Spanish ganar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *wardiānem. Doublet of guàrdia.
Inherited from Old Catalan guatla, from Vulgar Latin *quacla or *coacla, from contraction of a Late Latin quaccola. Compare Occitan catla and calha, French quaille.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *werrizāre. Derivable from guerra (“war”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hortāle, from hortus (“garden”).
From Vulgar Latin identitātem, from Classical Latin idem (“same, the same”).
Inherited from Old Catalan illa, from Vulgar Latin *isula (compare Occitan illa~iscla, French île, Spanish isla), from Latin īnsula (compare Portuguese ínsua).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *īliāta, from Latin īlia, plural of īle (“guts, intestines”). Spanish ijada.
Inherited from Old Catalan aïmant, from Vulgar Latin *adimantem, alteration of Latin adamantem (“adamant”).

parole.significato: (somebody) to lie down, as in preparation for sleep or sexual relations
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan jaure, from a pre-literary */ˈd͡ʒad͡z(e)re/, from Vulgar Latin *iacĕre, from Latin iacēre.

Inherited from Old Catalan jo~io~yo, from Vulgar Latin eō (attested from the sixth century), from Latin ego, from Proto-Italic *egō, from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂; akin to Greek εγώ (egó), Sanskrit अहम् (aham), all from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂. Compare Occitan jo, Spanish yo, French je, Italian i

parole.significato: sand smelt (any one of several small saltwater fish in the genus Atherina)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *juliellus, diminutive of iulis (“rainbow wrasse”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta. Documented from 1283–5. By surface analysis, jorn + -ada.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *iuvenciānus, from Latin iuvencus (“young”). A derivation from Proto-Celtic *yuwankos has also been proposed on account of the suffix.
Learned borrowing from Vulgar Latin jūdicātūra.
From Vulgar Latin *blatella, variant of *blattula, diminutive of blatta (“moth”). The initial consonant was apparently influenced by latus (“wide”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lacartum, from Latin lacertum.
Inherited from Old Catalan lagosta, from Vulgar Latin lacusta, alteration of Latin locusta, of uncertain origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lacrimizāre. Synchronically llàgrima (“teardrop”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: to lick (of a dam, particularly a ewe, towards her young)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lambinare, frequentive of Latin lambō (“to lick”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lampicāre, a frequentative verb based on Latin lampas (“lamp, torch”), of Greek origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lampūca, from lampas (“lamp; torch”). Or perhaps from Ancient Greek λάμπουσα (lámpousa), present active participle of λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lappācea, from lappāceus, from lappa (“burdock”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin labōrem (“agricultural work”), from Latin labor (“work”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Classical Latin laqueus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lēnicāre (“go smoothly”), from lēnis (“soft, smooth”).

parole.significato: language (the ability to communicate using words)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan lenguatge, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum. Attested in the Llibre de contemplació.

Inherited from Old Catalan *lentiyla (plural attested as lentiyles), from Vulgar Latin *lenticla (compare Occitan lentilha, French lentille, Spanish lenteja), syncopated form of Latin lenticula, diminutive of lēns. Compare lentícula, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lentisclus, from Latin lentīscus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lactitiōne, alteration of *lacticīnus from lac, lactis (“milk”). Compare lacticīnium (“milk product”). Feeding these plants to livestock was once thought to promote lactation.

parole.significato: slight; partial; not whole; not entire
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan leuger, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from *levius + -ārius, the former element representing an alteration of Latin levis (“lightweight”). Compare Occitan leugièr, French léger.
Inherited from Old Catalan levadís, from Vulgar Latin *levātīcius, from Latin levāre. By surface analysis, llevat + -ís.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *labrellum, diminutive of lābrum (“bathtub, basin”).
From a presumed masculine variant of Vulgar Latin limāca, from Latin līmāx.

From older llinyatge (via palatal dissimilation of /ʎ–ɲ/ to /ʎ–n/), from Old Catalan linyatge (via regular palatalization of initial /l/), from Vulgar Latin *līneāticum, from Latin līnea (“line, thread”).
Uncertain; perhaps from Vulgar Latin/Proto-Romance *līsius, a borrowing from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese liso, French lisse, Italian liscio.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *alīcia. Compare allec (“sardine”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lista, from Proto-West Germanic *līstā.

Inherited from Old Catalan lombrigol, from Vulgar Latin *umbilīculus (with /l-/ via agglutination from a definite article), diminutive of Latin umbilīcus. For the influence of preceding determiners, cf. French nombril and Romanian buric.

Inherited from Old Catalan longaniça, from Vulgar Latin *longanīcia, from Latin lūcānica (via substitution of the ending and analogy with longus). Cognate to Spanish longaniza and Portuguese lingüiça.
Inherited from Old Catalan lorer, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, suffixed form of Latin laurus. Compare Occitan laurièr.
From unattested Vulgar Latin *laurīcō, diminutive of laurex (“young of the rabbit”).
From Vulgar Latin lūcānīnus by dissimilation.
Inherited from Old Catalan luyr, from Vulgar Latin *lūcīre, from Latin lūcēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūcta, from Latin lūctor.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longiter. Compare Occitan lonhdan, Italian lontano, French lointain.
Inherited from Old Catalan lur, from Vulgar Latin *illūrum, from Latin illōrum (literally “of them”). Cognate to French leur, Italian loro.
From Vulgar Latin *lantada, from lampada, accusative of Latin lampas (“lamp, lantern”), with influence from lanterna.

Inherited from Old Catalan ludria, from Vulgar Latin *lutria, from Latin lutra. Compare Occitan luria~loira, Spanish lutria~nutria, Asturian llóndriga. The Vulgar Latin form was influenced by Ancient Greek ἔνυδρις (énudris).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *illu, from Latin illum, accusative of ille.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *maccare. (Compare Italian ammaccare, Spanish macar.) Ultimate origin unknown.

parole.significato: a company of armed men in the service of a lord
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan maisnada, maisonada, from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, from Latin mānsiō ("dwelling"). In the sense of "children", it originally meant all children in a particular household.
From Vulgar Latin *male-habitidiare, from male habĭtus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *macla (“mesh”), from Latin macula (“spot, stain”). Doublet of màcula, a learned borrowing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manizāre. By surface analysis, man- (“hand”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *man(u)āria, from the feminine of Latin manuārius. Compare Occitan manièra, Spanish manera, Portuguese maneira, French manière.
From Vulgar Latin *manificium, from Latin manificus (“handmade”), from manus (“hand”) and -ficus, related to faciō (“to make”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mānsus, from Latin mānsuetus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mānsus.

parole.significato: to maintain; to uphold; to keep going
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan mantenir, from Vulgar Latin *mantenīre, infinitive of *manteniō (“to support”), variant of Late Latin manuteneō, corresponding to Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mania (“manual skill”), from Latin manus (“hand”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin masclus, from Latin masculus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *massīcius. By surface analysis, massa + -ís.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mattiāna, shortened from māla mattiāna, plural of mālum mattiānum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin melica, from Latin medica (“Median”). Compare Italian meliga.
From Vulgar Latin *mercuriāgo, from Mercurius (“Mercury”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin melica, from Latin medica (“Median”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *milva, alternation of Latin milvus (“gurnard”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mīna, *mēna, from Gaulish *meina (“mineral, ore”). Doublet of mina (“mine”). First attested in 1185.
From Vulgar Latin *minuus, related to minor (“less”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mentōnem, an augmentative of Latin mentum (“chin”). Compare French menton.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *minuscapāre. Cognate with Portuguese menoscabar.
From Vulgar Latin *minus caput.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *merēscere, from Latin merēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *misculātīcius, derived from Early Medieval Latin *misculāre. By surface analysis, mesclat + -ís.

parole.significato: field guard (an armed guard appointed to keep watch over crops)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *messicārius, from Latin messis (“harvest”).
Inherited from Old Catalan mica, from Vulgar Latin *mīcca, from Latin mīca (“crumb”) with expression gemination of /k/. Compare Occitan mica and Aragonese mica.
Inherited from Old Catalan milà, from Vulgar Latin *mīlvānus, derived from Latin mī̆lvus. Compare melva.

Inherited from Old Catalan mirall~mirayl, from Vulgar Latin *mīrāclum (“mirror”), derived from Latin mīrārī (“look at”). By surface analysis, mirar + -all. Compare Occitan miralh, Old French mirail. Morphological doublet of miracle, a borrowing from Latin.

Inherited from Old Catalan moyl, from Vulgar Latin *medullum, analogically derived from Latin medulla, and probably influenced by Etymology 1. Compare Occitan mesolh, Spanish meollo, Portuguese miolo. Doublet of molla and medul·la, which were, respectively, inherited and borrowed from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos. Cognate with French mouton.

Inherited from Old Catalan mon, from Vulgar Latin *mum, reduced form of Latin meum, from Proto-Italic *meos. Compare Occitan and French mon. In unstressed position in Vulgar Latin meum, meam etc. were monosyllabic and regularly became mon, ma etc. in Catalan. When stressed they were disyllabic and b

parole.significato: monestrell (red grape variety originating in Catalonia)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin monastēriellum, diminutive of monastērium (“monastery”), presumably due to being cultivated on monastery grounds.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from mōrum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin morena, from Latin haemorrhoidae, from Ancient Greek αἱμορροΐς (haimorrhoḯs). Doublet of hemorroide, a learned borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *mercuriolis, variant of mercuriālis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *murrum, of unknown origin. Perhaps onomatopoeic.

parole.significato: to move (to cause to change place or posture in any manner; to set in motion)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *movĕre, from Latin movēre. Compare Occitan mòure.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *movitīcius, from Latin movēre.

Inherited from Old Catalan mullar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“soften by soaking”), a verb derived ultimately from Latin mollis (“soft”). Cognate with French mouiller, Occitan molhar, Spanish mojar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *montāre, from Latin montem (“mountain”).

parole.significato: an owl, especially the little owl (Athene noctua)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *noctuolus, diminutive of noctua (“owl”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *noctiola, alteration of Vulgar Latin *noctuola, from Latin noctua.
Variant of earlier musti, from Vulgar Latin *mustidus, from mustum (“must”).
From Vulgar Latin *nato, *natōnem, diminutive of natus (“born”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *natta, from Latin matta.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nepōta, feminized counterpart of Latin nepōtem (“nephew”). Compare Occitan neboda, Romanian nepoată.
From Vulgar Latin nequitosus, from inīquitās.
From Vulgar Latin *ninnus.

From Old Catalan net, from Vulgar Latin *nittus, syncopated from Latin nitidus (“bright, clear”). Doublet of nèdol ('pasturage'), from Old Catalan nèdeu (“clean”), from nitidus- but without the early syncope. Compare also French net, Italian netto.

Restructuring, based on net (“clean”), of Old Catalan nedejar, from Vulgar Latin *nitidiāre, a verb based on Latin nitidus (“shining, polished”), which subsequently came to mean 'clean'. For similar restructurings, cf. Occitan netejar and French nettoyer (replacing Old Occitan nedejar and Old French
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nĕvem, alteration of Latin nivem.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nevāre, ultimately from Latin nivem (“snow”, noun).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *naucus (“trough”), from *naucula, diminutive of Latin navis (“ship”).
Inherited from Old Catalan noces, from Vulgar Latin *nŏptiās, alteration of Latin nuptiās.
Unknown. Proposals include: # Vulgar Latin *novius (“newly wed”) # Vulgar Latin *novinus, a diminutive of novus (“new”) # from a diminutive of nin (a variant form of nen), i.e. nin > ninoi > noi
Inherited from Old Catalan noli, nolit, from Vulgar Latin *naulium, from Latin naulum, from Ancient Greek ναῦλον (naûlon).
Inherited from Old Catalan nora, from Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nŏcem, alteration of Latin nucem. Compare Occitan nòtz, Spanish nuez, Portuguese noz.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nocĕre, from Latin nocēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *novius (“newly wed”). Doublet of nòvio.
Inherited from Old Catalan obert~ubert, from Vulgar Latin *opertus (compare Occitan obert~dobert, French ouvert), alteration of Latin apertus (compare Spanish abierto).

Inherited from Old Catalan obertura, from Vulgar Latin *opertūra (compare Occitan obertura~dobertura, French ouverture), alteration of Latin apertūra (compare Spanish abertura). By surface analysis, obert + -ura. Doublet of the borrowed form apertura. The sense of "aperture" was a later learned deve
From Vulgar Latin *oclāta, from Latin oculāta.
Inherited from Old Catalan oblidar, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, a frequentative based on Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus). Compare Occitan oblidar.
Inherited from Old Catalan obrir, from Vulgar Latin *operīre, from Latin aperīre (influenced by cooperīre). Compare Occitan obrir~dobrir, Aragonese obrir~ubrir, French ouvrir, Spanish abrir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.

parole.significato: offer (a proposal that has been made)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *offerta, from the female past participle of Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre (which had the past participle oblāta). First attested in the 13th century.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *olīvus, from Latin olīva, olīvum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *implīre, from Latin implēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aunclum, from Latin avunculus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *undizāre. By surface analysis, ona + -ejar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aurāticum, derived from Latin aura (“wind, breeze”). By surface analysis, ora + -atge.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aurizāre. Equivalent to ora + -ejar.

Probably from metathesis of Old Catalan *eroneta, from Vulgar Latin *hirundĭtta, a diminutive of Latin hirundō. The suffix may have also been an internal formation within early Catalan: compare the different suffixes used in nearby Romance cognates: Occitan ironda, randoleta, irondela, Spanish golon
Variant form of orèndola, from Vulgar Latin *hirundula, diminutive of hirundō (“swallow”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *orgollium, borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgōllju.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aurīna, alteration of Latin ūrīna. Medieval Catalan also had a variant urina, matching the original Latin form.
From Vulgar Latin urinal.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *ōrula, diminutive of Latin ōra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hormizāre.
Assimilated form of orenella, metathesised from Old Catalan *eronella, from Vulgar Latin *hirundella, diminutive of hirundō (“swallow”).

From Vulgar Latin *hordeāta, itself derived from Latin hordeum (“barley”). How the word entered Catalan is disputed. Some see it as originating in the Valencian dialect (and making its way into Spanish (horchata) possibly via a Mozarabic source), but the word was only attested in Catalan around the
Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin pagellus, diminutive of Latin phager (“sea bream”).
Inherited from Old Catalan paladar, from Vulgar Latin *palātārem, derived from Latin palātum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from the accusative form of Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “log, trunk, body of soldiers, etc.”).

parole.significato: a parasol mushroom, especially the highly edible Macrolepiota procera
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus, palumbēs (“wood pigeon”). Cognate with Sicilian palumma.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *panecaldum.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pānucla < pānucula, alternative form of Latin pānicula, diminutive of pānus (“ear of millet”). Cognate with Spanish panoja (“ear of grain”), Italian pannocchia (“corncob, ear”).
Earlier pantaixar, from Vulgar Latin *pantasiāre (“to have a nightmare”), from Ancient Greek φαντασιόω (phantasióō, “to hallucinate”), from φαντασία (phantasía, “appearance, image, fantasy”).
Uncertain. Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *palathella, a metathesised diminutive of Latin lapathum (“a kind of sorrel”).

parole.significato: Parmesan (of, from or relating to Parma)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *parmēsānus. Compare French parmesan.

parole.significato: to appear, to seem, to look like
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre. Doublet of parer (noun).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pascua, from Late Latin pascha (influenced by pascua 'pastures, grazing', perhaps because of the bitter herbs of the Passover seder or the end of fasting for Lent at Easter), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), ultimately from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésakh, “Passover”).

parole.significato: to pass, to pass by, to go by (to move past)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá). Doublet of pastitxo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pitaccium, variant of Latin pittacium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin pica, variant form of Latin pix (“pitch, tar”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pilūc(i)cāre, ultimately from Latin pilāre (“remove hair”). The regular outcome in Catalan would have been *pelucar; the ⟨ll⟩ /ʎ/ was taken from pell (“skin, pelt”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pennellus, masculinized diminutive of penna (“feather, wing”). The failure of Latin /nn/ to yield the expected */ɲ/ in Catalan may be due to palatal dissimilation from the following /ʎ/ < /ll/.
Inherited from Old Catalan penjar, from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, a frequentative of Latin pendere. Same as Occitan penjar and Aragonese penchar

parole.significato: a hanging cluster of flowers or fruits, a bunch
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *penduculus, from *pendicāre, from pendeō (“to hang down”). The j is due to the influence of penjar (“hang”), another derivation from *pendicāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pectinī̆culum, diminutive of Latin pecten (“comb”).
Probably from Vulgar Latin *pectinella, from Latin pecten (“comb; scallop”).
Inherited from Old Catalan pera, from Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular.
From pera + -er, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *pirārius (cf. Medieval Latin pirarius), from Latin pirus. Compare French poirier.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pergamīnus.
Inherited from Old Catalan perill, from Vulgar Latin *periclu(m), syncopated form of Latin perīculum. Compare Occitan perilh, French péril.
From Old Catalan peroliar, from Vulgar Latin peroleare, alteration of Latin peroleō (“I emit a penetrating odour”).

Inherited from Old Catalan peyrol, from Vulgar Latin *pariolum, diminutive of *parium, from Transalpine Gaulish parios, from Proto-Celtic *kʷaryos (“cauldron”). Compare Welsh pair and Irish coire. By surface analysis, pèr + -ol.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *persequīre, from Latin persequī.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pestellus, diminutive of Late Latin pestulus, alteration of Latin pessulus. Cognate with Spanish pestillo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin pittitus, an expressive creation (with variant forms pitinnus, pitulus, piccinus, pitikkus, etc.). Compare Occitan and French petit.

parole.significato: to step on, set foot on
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pedicāre, from Latin ped- (“foot”) + -icāre (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: bootee (a soft, woolen shoe, usually knitted, for a baby or small pet)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *pedūcus, from Latin pēs, pedis (“foot”).
Inherited from Old Catalan picar, from Vulgar Latin *pīccāre, itself a derivative of Latin pīcus or of onomatopoeic origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin petulāre, a back-formation from petulāns.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, from Latin pīla (“pillar”).
From Vulgar Latin *pilotta, diminutive of pila. Compare French pelote, Spanish pelota.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pinciānus from an onomatopoeic *pink representing the sound of its call.
From the feminine of Vulgar Latin pīnctus, from Latin pictus, perfect passive participle of pingō (“to paint”).
Inherited from Old Catalan pintar, from Vulgar Latin *pinctāre < *pictāre, frequentative from Latin pingere.
Inherited from Old Catalan pintor, from Vulgar Latin *pīnctōrem, from Latin pictōrem. Compare Occitan pintor, Spanish pintor, French peintre.
Inherited from Old Catalan pintura, from Vulgar Latin *pinctūra, from Latin pictūra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīpa (“pipe”), from Latin pīpō (“to pip”).

parole.significato: a blow with the chest; a chest bump
parole.testo: By surface analysis, pit + -ada. The presence of medial r suggests either derivation from a Vulgar Latin *pectorata or influence from the verb apitrar (“to hit with the chest”).

parole.significato: to piss; to pee; to urinate
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, of echoic origin.
Inherited from Old Catalan plansó, from Vulgar Latin *plantiōnem, from Latin planta. Compare Occitan plançon.
Substantivization of the archaic adjective plat (“flat”), from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús). Compare French plat.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plicātīcius, from Latin plicāre. By surface analysis, plegat + -ís.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plicta, aphaeretic and contracted form of applicita, perfect passive participle of applicō (“to attach”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plovia.
Inherited from Old Catalan poder, from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.
From Vulgar Latin *putriō, from Latin putreō (“I am rotten”).
Past participle of podrir (“rot”), from Vulgar Latin *putrīre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pūlegiolum, diminutive of Latin pūlegium.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of Latin pullus. Compare French poule, Spanish polla, Romanian pulă.

parole.significato: any poplar tree, especially the black poplar (Populus nigra)
parole.testo: Probably from pollanca < pollanc, from poll (“poplar”), from Vulgar Latin *pōclus, from alteration and contraction of Latin pōpulus (“poplar”).
Probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *pollicāria, from Latin pollicāris.
From a Vulgar Latin *pollicō, from Latin pollex (“thumb”).

Inherited from Old Catalan pols, from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, from Latin pulvis (reassigned to the neuter gender), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”). Doublet of pólvera, from the Vulgar Latin plural *pulvera.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *pullitrus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *puppa, from Latin puppis (“stern”), possibly with influence from prora (“prow”).
Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin porclaca, from Latin portulaca.
From Vulgar Latin portulānus, from portus (“port”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin postus, from positus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appostīcius, from appositus < apponō.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pottum, pottus (“pot, jar”), from Frankish *pott, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot”), from Proto-Indo-European *budnós (“a type of vessel”). Cognate with French pot, English pot, Saterland Frisian Pot, Dutch pot, German Low German Pott, German Pott, Swedish potta (“chamb
From Vulgar Latin *pauta. First attested in 1371.
From dialectal potina (“hodgepodge”), from Vulgar Latin *pultina, from puls (“porridge”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin prebyteru.
From Vulgar Latin *prōgenitūra, from Latin prōgignō (“to beget”).
From Vulgar Latin *provinca, alteration of Latin pervinca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prūdīre, dissimilated from Latin prūrīre. First attested in 1371.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prūniōne, from Latin prūnum.
Inherited from Old Catalan pudir, from Vulgar Latin *pūtīre, from Latin pūtēre (with a change in verb class).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pūlicōnem, from Latin pūlicem (“flea”). Compare Spanish pulgón, Portuguese pulgão.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *postius.

parole.significato: to rise, go up, ascend, climb up
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *podiāre, a verb based on Latin podium. Compare Occitan pujar, Aragonese puyar.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *pūtta, of uncertain origin, perhaps derived from Latin *puta, female form of Latin putus (“teeny boy”), a hapax legomenon of dubious reading. Cognate with French pute, Spanish puta, Portuguese puta, Galician puta, Asturian puta, as well as Old Italian putta (“girl”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pampulus, from Latin pampinus.
Inherited from Old Catalan pèr (“cauldron”), from Vulgar Latin *parium, from Transalpine Gaulish parios, from Proto-Celtic *kʷaryos. Cognate to Irish coire, Welsh pair.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *perdita, a noun based on the feminine of Latin perditus (“lost”), from perdere (“lose”). Compare Occitan pèrda~pèrdia, French perte, Spanish pérdida.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pisulum, diminutive of pisum (“pea”).

parole.significato: curd (the part of milk that coagulates when it sours)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan quayl, from Vulgar Latin *quaglum, from Latin coagulum. Compare Occitan calh, Spanish cuajo. Doublet of col and coàgul, a borrowing.
Inherited from Old Catalan quayllar, from Vulgar Latin quāglāre, from Latin coāgulāre. Compare Occitan calhar, French cailler, Spanish cuajar. Doublet of coagular, a borrowing from Latin.
From Vulgar Latin *capseum (“chin”). Compare Occitan cais (“jaw”) and Portuguese queixo (“chin”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin caria, from Latin cariēs (“decay”).
From Vulgar Latin *rāpācea, a derivation from rāpum (“turnip”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rapidium, from rapidus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rādīcārius, from rādīx (“root”).

parole.significato: to scrape (off) (remove something from a surface)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rāsicāre, a frequentative verb based on Latin rāsus (“shaven”).

parole.significato: to scrape (draw a sharp object along a surface)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *raspāre, from Frankish *hraspōn.
Uncertain. From Old Catalan ralla, raylla; perhaps a deverbal from ratllar, from Vulgar Latin *rallare or *radulare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *radulare, from radula (“file”). Equivalent to ratlla + -ar. Compare Spanish rayar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rādīcia, from Latin rādō (“to scrape”).

parole.significato: to burst, explode, blow up, break
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *repentare, from Latin repēns (“sudden, unexpected”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *repullus (“sprout”), from pullus (“chick”). Cognate with Galician rebolo, Spanish rebollo.
From Vulgar Latin *recaptō, alteration of Latin accapitō. Cognate with Venetan regatar.
From Vulgar Latin *reminctulare, derived from Latin mingō (“I urinate”).

parole.significato: to dig up, to turn over (land)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *removĕre, from Latin removēre. Compare moure. First attested in the 13th century.
From Vulgar Latin *rehinnitulāre, prefixed form of *hinnītulare, from Latin hinnītus (“neigh”), from hinniō (“to neigh, to whinny”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ringīre, from Latin ringī.
From lleparassa via metathesis, and this in turn from llapassa, from Vulgar Latin *lappācea, from lappāceus, from lappa (“burdock”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin reprēsalia, from reprehēnsus (“seized”). Compare French représaille, Italian rappresaglia.
From Vulgar Latin reproprium, variant form of opprobrium.

parole.significato: weir, barrage (an obstruction placed across a waterway)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *resclausa, variant of reclausa (“closed”) from clausus.

parole.significato: to resow, to plant the same crop again in the same field
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *restupulare, from Latin stupula, alteration of stipula (“stubble”). Cognate to rostollar.
From a Vulgar Latin *retronnīre, blend of Latin retinnīre (“resound”) and tonitrus (“thunder”).
Inherited from Old Catalan reviscolar, from Vulgar Latin *revīvisculāre, derived from Latin revīvīscere.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *rīsuālia, as a neuter plural derived from Latin rīsus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rīvāria, from the feminine of Vulgar Latin *rīvārius, from rīvus (“stream, channel”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“boil, churn”).
Inherited from Old Catalan riu, from Vulgar Latin rius (“river”), from Latin rīvus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós, from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move, set in motion”) + *-wós.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rotulare, from rotula (“roll”), diminutive of rota (“wheel”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ruiu, from Latin rubeus, derivative of ruber. Compare Occitan roge, French rouge, Franco-Provençal rojo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *roretŭriu, from Latin rhus tyrius (“Tyrian sumac”), a name originally applied to the tanner's sumac, Rhus coriaria.
Inherited from Old Catalan romanir (compare Occitan remàner), from Vulgar Latin *remanĕre, as a variant, with change in conjugation, of Latin remanēre. Compare Old French remaindre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rŭmĭcāria, from rŭmex (“sorrel”).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *rōmārius, a noun based on rōs (“dew”) + maris (“of the sea”), equivalent of Latin rōsmarīnus. Compare Spanish romero.
From earlier romèscol, from *remescle, from Vulgar Latin *remisculus, from misculō (“mix”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aerūgna, from Latin aerūginem, accusative of aerūgo.

Inherited from Old Catalan renyó~ronyó, from Vulgar Latin *rōniōnem~*rēniōnem, derived from Latin rēn, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰren- (“an internal part of the body”). Compare Aragonese rinyón, Occitan renhon, ronhon; French rognon, Spanish riñón.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rubipectus, from rubeus (“red”) + pectus (“breast”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōsāta, derived from Latin rōs.
Inherited from Old Catalan rosegar, from Vulgar Latin *rōsicāre, frequentative based on Latin rōdere, whence obsolete Catalan roure.
From Vulgar Latin *rossa.
From Vulgar Latin *rusciniolus, from Vulgar Latin lusciniola, diminutive of Classical Latin luscinia.

parole.significato: stubble (the short stalks left in a field after crops have been harvested)
parole.testo: Assimilated form of earlier restoll, from Vulgar Latin *restuculu(m), a variant of *restupulu(m) from Latin stupula, a variant of stipula (“stalk, stubble”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ruptāre, modification of Latin ructāre.
Inherited from Old Catalan roveyl, from Vulgar Latin *rōbĭclus, diminutive based on Latin rōbīgō (“rust”). First attested in the 13th century. Compare Occitan rovilh, French rouille, Spanish robín.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *rubeolus, a diminutive of Latin rubeus (“red”); or an alternation of rovellol from rovell (“rust”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōscidāre, derived from Latin rōscidus. Compare Portuguese and Spanish rociar.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *rubeola via Mozarabic.
