parole.significato: to know (a fact), to have knowledge
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan saber, from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapĕre (“taste, know”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *satullāre, diminutive of Latin saturāre. Compare French souler and Italian satollare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *saginu(m), from Latin sagina. Doublet of saïm.
Inherited from Old Catalan salar, from Vulgar Latin *salāre, a verb based on Latin sāl (“salt”) (compare Classical salire). Cognate with Occitan salar, French saler, Spanish salar.
Vulgar Latin *salma, from Latin sagma.
From Vulgar Latin salisparsōrium, salsparsōrium, from Vulgar Latin *salsparsiō, *salsparsiō, from sal (“salt”) and sparsiō (“sprinkling”).
Inherited from Old Catalan salsa, from Vulgar Latin *salsa, a noun based on the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), perfect passive participle of salīre, a verb based on sāl.
Inherited from Old Catalan salvatge, from Vulgar Latin salvāticus, variant of Latin silvāticus (showing assimilation). Doublet of selvàtic, a learned borrowing via Italian.

Inherited from Old Catalan sang~sanch, from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Classical Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Its gender could also be masculine in Old Catalan, as it was in Latin. Compare Occitan sang, French sang, Si
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *singluttus, a blend of gluttīre (“to swallow”) + Latin singultus (“a hiccup”). Compare French sanglot, Italian singhiozzo and Occitan sanglòt.
From Vulgar Latin *singluttāre, from Latin singultāre via metathesis, or derived from sanglot + -ar. Compare Occitan sanglotar, French sangloter; cf. also Spanish sollozar, Italian singhiozzare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin sanguineolus, diminutive of sanguineus (“bloody”), from the reddish colour of the leaves and stems in fall and winter.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapium (“wise”), from Latin sapidus (“delicious, wise”). Despite the spelling, no dialect shows a pronunciation with /v/. The expected spelling with ⟨b⟩ is attested in Old Catalan.

parole.significato: lard (rendered animal fat, especially pork fat)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *sagīmen, from Latin sagīna. Doublet of sagí. Compare Spanish saín.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sepullīre, alteration of Latin sepeliō (“to bury”).
Inherited from Old Catalan seguir, from Vulgar Latin *sequĕre (with a change in conjugation), regularization of Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

parole.significato: a wooden bucket resembling a horizontally bisected barrel with handles used for harvesting grapes
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *semālis (“divided in half”), from semis (“half”).
Inherited from Old Catalan sen, from Vulgar Latin *sennus, from Frankish *sinn, possibly influenced by Latin sensus (“sense”).

parole.significato: to squeeze (e.g. someone's hand); to clench (one's teeth)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin serrāre (“to close”). First attested in the 14th century.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sĕdicum.

Inherited from Old Catalan fivella, from Vulgar Latin *fībella, diminutive of Latin fībula. The reason for the change in the initial consonant is unclear, but it is reflected in several other Romance varieties as well. Doublet of fíbula, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *supergus, alteration of superbus. Doublet of superb, a learned borrowing.

Inherited from Old Catalan sobirà (also subirà, sobiran), from Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super. Cognate with Occitan sobeiran, French souverain, Spanish soberano. Doublet of soprano, which was borrowed from Italian.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *suffrigere, *subfrigere, from sub- (“under”) and frīgō (“to roast, fry, parch”).

parole.significato: to tolerate, to accept, to put up with
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan sofrir~soferir, from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre (whence the Old Catalan variant soferre).

parole.significato: sole (the bottom of a shoe or boot)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *sola, from Latin solea.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sōliculus, diminutive of Latin sōl.
From sumoll, from sumollar (“to dry out”), from Vulgar Latin submolliāre, from mollis (“soft”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *submerguliare, a blend of Latin summergō (“to submerge”) with *merguliō (“diver”). Cognate with Spanish somorgujar.
Inherited from Old Catalan somriure~sumriure, from Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre. Compare Occitan sorire.

Inherited from Old Catalan son, from Vulgar Latin sum, reduced form of Latin suum, accusative of suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos. Compare Occitan and French son. In unstressed position in Vulgar Latin suum, suam etc. were monosyllabic and regularly became son, sa etc. in Catalan. When stressed they w
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sonāculum, from Latin sonāre (“make noise”). By surface analysis, sonar + -all. Doublet of sonalla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subpluvius, from sub- (“under”) and pluvia (“rain”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorbīre, from Latin sorbēre.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *subrotulāre, from Latin rotula (“small wheel”).

parole.significato: the ring used in ring jousting
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorticula (“small object for casting lots”), diminutive of sors (“fate”). Cognate with Galician sortella, Spanish sortija.
Inherited from Old Catalan sota, from Vulgar Latin *subta, alteration of Latin subtus (whence Old Catalan sots), derived from sub, from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *subtāna, derived from subtus (“below, beneath”). The clothing sense is certainly borrowed from Italian sottana.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tacca, compare French tache.
From earlier Old Catalan tanasida, from Vulgar Latin tanacetum, perhaps from tenax (“tenacious”).

Inherited from Old Catalan tastar, perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *tastāre, from older *taxitāre, frequentative based on Late Latin taxāre, derived from Classical Latin tangere (“touch”). Compare Occitan tastar, Italian tastare, Old French taster.
From Vulgar Latin *tīnalia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *turbinīnus, diminutive of Latin turbinem, with dissimilation of n to l and metathesis of e and o.

parole.significato: earthly, worldly (relating to the earth or this world, as opposed to heaven)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *terrēnālis. First attested in the 14th century. By surface analysis, Latin terrēnus + -al. Compare terrestre.
Inherited from Old Catalan terreny, from some Vulgar Latin form such as *terrignum, *terrĭnĕus, or *terrēnĕus. In any case, ultimately from Latin terra (“land”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *toccāre, *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tumānīnus, diminutive of Vulgar Latin *tumānia, *thȳmānea, from thȳmiāma (“incense”), borrowing of Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama).

Inherited from Old Catalan ton, from Vulgar Latin *tum, reduced form of Latin tuum, from Proto-Italic *towos. Compare Occitan and French ton. In unstressed position in Vulgar Latin tuum, tuam etc. were monosyllabic and regularly became ton, ta etc. in Catalan. When stressed they were disyllabic and
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tondĕre, variant of Latin tondēre. Cognate with French tondre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *thunnīna. Compare Spanish tonina, toñina.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tornātīcius, from Latin tornāre. By surface analysis, tornat + -ís.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *turritānus, from turris (“tower”).
From Vulgar Latin *tortilaginem, from Latin tortilis (“twisted, coiled”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Classical Latin tōtus.

parole.significato: to pour into another container, to decant
parole.testo: Either from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcāre, from fricō (“to rub”), or from *transfaecare, from faex (“sediment”). Cognate with Galician trasfegar, Spanish trasegar, Portuguese trasfegar.
From Vulgar Latin *tragella, alteration of Latin trāgula. Doublet of tralla.
Inherited from Old Catalan traginar, from Vulgar Latin *tragināre, from Latin trahō. Compare Occitan treginar, French traîner.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trāgla, from Latin trāgula (“javelin”).
From Vulgar Latin *tractiāre.
Inherited from Old Catalan treballar, trabaylar, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device”).
From earlier tremoló, a contraction of tremolaó, from Vulgar Latin *tremulātiōnem, from tremulus (“trembling”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trēna, from Latin trīna (“triple”).
From Vulgar Latin *tresaurus, a variant of Classical Latin thesaurus; from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós). Doublet of tesaurus.

parole.significato: to take out, take off, take down
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan traure, apparently from a Vulgar Latin *tracĕre (for the sound-changes, compare Latin dīcĕre > Catalan diure), from Latin trahere (“to draw, drag”). First attested in the 16th century.
Inherited from Old Catalan trist, from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis. Compare Occitan triste.

Inherited from Old Catalan tro, from Vulgar Latin *tronus, a noun based on Vulgar Latin *tronāre, modification of Latin tonāre (“to thunder”) (with the additional /r/ perhaps by analogy with *tronitus, metathesis of tonitrus). Compare Spanish trueno, Portuguese trom.
Inherited from Old Catalan trobador, from Vulgar Latin *tropātōrem, agent noun based on Vulgar Latin *tropare, probably from Latin tropus, of Greek origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torca, from Latin torquis (“collar, wreath”).

Inherited from Old Catalan tronar, from Vulgar Latin *tronāre, from Latin tonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). Additional /r/ likely taken from *tronitus, metathesis of Latin tonitrus. Compare Occitan tronar, Spanish tronar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trūdicāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *troculum, from Latin torculum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *titōne, from Latin titus.

Inherited from Old Catalan tèrbol, from Vulgar Latin *turbulus, probably an alteration of Latin turbidus, with influence from turbulentus. The current form of the Catalan word was likely influenced by the verb terbolar, from an earlier *torbolar, from a Vulgar Latin *turbulāre (cf. Occitan trebolar,
Inherited from Old Catalan tòfera, from Vulgar Latin *tufera, variant of Latin tūbera. Doublet of trufa.
Inherited from Old Catalan tòrcer~torçre, from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre, from Latin torquēre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ūlŭlare (with dissimilation of /l–l/), modified from Latin ŭlŭlāre. Doublet of ulular, a borrowing from Latin. Compare Occitan udolar, ulodar; French hurler; Spanish aullar.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus, from Proto-Italic *okelos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Compare Occitan uèlh, French œil, Spanish ojo, Portuguese olho, Italian occhio. Doublet of òcul, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oculāta, ultimately from Latin oculus (“eye”). By surface analysis, ull + -ada.

From Vulgar Latin vāscella, from the neuter plural of Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of Latin vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vessel”). Compare Occitan vaissella, French vaisselle, Spanish vajilla, Portuguese baixela, Sicilian vasceḍḍa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vicāta, from Latin vicis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vissīna.
Inherited from Old Catalan vela, from Vulgar Latin *vēla, from the plural of Latin vēlum, reinterpreted as a feminine singular.
Inherited from Old Catalan vell~veyl, from Vulgar Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus, diminutive of vetus. Compare Occitan vièlh, French vieux, Spanish viejo.

parole.significato: fleece; the wool of a woolly animal, such as a sheep
parole.testo: Probably an alteration of Old Catalan véllor, from Vulgar Latin *vellōrem, from Latin vellerem. Cf. also Spanish vellón.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ventrisca, from Latin venter (“belly”).

parole.significato: a plot of land, especially a sown field clearly distinguishable from the ones adjoining it
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *variāle, from Latin varius.
From verd + -ura or Vulgar Latin *virdūra.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *virdiārium, syncopated form of Latin viridiārium, variant of viridārium, from viridis (“green”).
Inherited from Old Catalan vergonya, from Vulgar Latin *vergunnia, from Latin verecundia. Compare Occitan vergonha, French vergogne, Italian vergogna, now-obsolete Spanish vergüeña.
From Vulgar Latin *vīcīnātus or veí + -at.
From Vulgar Latin *venentem, from Latin venientem.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *veria, from Latin verua (“railing around an altar or tomb”).

parole.significato: to turn (to change one's direction of travel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *virāre, probably from Latin vibrāre (in which case it is a doublet of vibrar). Other possibilities include an alteration of gȳrō (source of the synonym girar) or a derivation from Gaulish *viru (“to deviate, veer off”), itself derived from viros (“round, crooked”). Compa
From Vulgar Latin *viriola, diminutive of viria (“bracelet”). French ferrule, English ferrule.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *variōnem, from varus (“pimple”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *visita, from Latin visa, feminine past participle of videō.

parole.significato: to sail around, to round, to circumnavigate
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volgere, from Latin volvō (“to roll, to tumble”). Cognate with Italian volgere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.
From the past participle of Old Catalan voldre, from Latin volvere. Corresponds to Vulgar Latin *voltus, from *volŭtus, from Latin volūtus.

parole.significato: to go round, go around, orbit
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exoffocatiōnem, from Latin offōcō (“to choke”).
Inherited from Old Catalan sarpellera, probably from Vulgar Latin *sirpiculāria, derived from Latin scirpiculus (from scirpus (“bullrush”)).
From earlier cerceta, from Vulgar Latin cercedula, Latin querquetula.
Inherited from Old Catalan cisclar, from Vulgar Latin *cisclāre, alteration of fistulāre (“to play the flute”). Compare Spanish chillar and Basque txistulari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exsubīliāre, from īlia (“lower abdomen”).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *exsuppāre, from Late Latin suppa, of Germanic origin. First attested in 1617.
